Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin
A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
Any form of physical contact with others

Threat.value: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
I am permanently an outsider now

issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: The social avoidance items are difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. These triggers imply avoidance of people linked to a discrete later-life event, but the trauma is chronic/developmental and caregiver-based; there is no corresponding trigger or appraisal content tying prior social contacts or specific intimacy-linked reminders to the abuse history.

issues.item: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
issues.explanation: Intrusion Monitoring suggests fear of an intruder entering the home, which fits home-invasion or stalking trauma better than childhood caregiver physical abuse. With no accompanying memory or trigger content about nighttime entry, footsteps, doors, or home intrusion, this threat item is hard to explain from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: No Good Ahead and Outsider are broad, depressive or social-identity appraisals, whereas the other active content is dominated by vigilance, bodily threat detection, and sensory triggering. This combination is not impossible, but here the intimacy/social avoidance items appear to depend on relational shame or alienation that is otherwise underdeveloped and weakly connected to the trigger/threat pattern, reducing coherence.

issues.item: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore
issues.explanation: Given the formulation, Triggers and Negative Appraisals should be tightly linked, but the chosen triggers are mainly tactile/somatic/intrusive-memory cues while two maladaptive strategies focus on avoiding social contacts and intimacy. Those strategies are not well supported by the trigger set and feel targeted at a different symptom cluster than the one represented elsewhere.

vignette:
Frank is a 66-year-old software engineer, married for over forty years, who came to therapy at his wife's gentle but persistent urging. He sat forward in the chair, hands resting on his knees, and described a life lived on high alert. He had always known something was different about him, but it was only in the last few months, after a series of small, inexplicable reactions, that the shape of it had begun to clarify.

The event itself had happened more than fifty years ago, in the basement of his childhood home. His father, a man whose moods could shift without warning, had cornered him there. Frank remembered the cold concrete against his bare legs, the smell of damp and furnace oil, and the specific, searing sensation of his father's hand-hot, flat, and hard-landing on the back of his neck. It wasn't the worst beating, but it was the one that had lodged itself permanently. The temperature of that hand, the way it felt like a brand on his skin, had become a fixed point in his memory. He could still feel it, sometimes, without warning. A memory that came not as a picture, but as a sudden, full-body flash: the cold floor, the hot palm, the heart pounding in his chest so hard he thought it would break his ribs.

He had learned, over the decades, to manage. As a software engineer, he found comfort in the predictable logic of code, in systems that followed rules. His work environment was controlled, quiet, and solitary. But even there, the vigilance never stopped. He scanned every room he entered, a habit so automatic he no longer noticed he was doing it. He noticed potential weapons everywhere: a letter opener on a desk, a heavy stapler, the sharp edge of a paper cutter in the supply closet. He didn't think of them as threats in a conscious way; his body simply registered them, catalogued them, before his mind had even caught up. He had come to believe that this was just how the world worked-that danger was always waiting, and that only constant, exhausting watchfulness kept him safe.

The consequences of this vigilance had crept into every corner of his life. He had stopped accepting social invitations years ago. Seeing people he had once enjoyed-colleagues from old projects, neighbors who waved from their driveways-now felt like a burden. He couldn't relax around them. He was certain they could see something wrong with him, that they could sense he was different, an outsider playing a part. He had come to believe, with a quiet and unshakeable certainty, that people could not be trusted. Not because they were malicious, but because they were unpredictable. And unpredictability was the thing he feared most.

The most difficult consequence, and the one that had finally brought him to therapy, was the toll it had taken on his marriage. He loved his wife, but he had built a wall of avoidance between them. He could not bear to be touched unexpectedly. A hand on his shoulder from behind would make him flinch, his body jerking away before his mind could register it was her. He had started to avoid physical contact altogether, pulling back from hugs, sitting at the far end of the couch. He had also, without really meaning to, begun to avoid looking at his own body. He dressed in the dark, avoided mirrors in the bathroom, and felt a deep, wordless aversion to the sensation of his own skin. He did not know why. He only knew that his body felt like a place where something bad had happened, and that paying attention to it was dangerous.

What frightened him most was the way his body reacted before he could think. A sudden noise, a door closing too hard, and his heart would be racing, his hands cold, before he even knew what had triggered it. He had spent his whole life trying to be in control, to be rational, to keep the world orderly. But his own body had become a source of chaos he could not manage. He came to therapy not because he believed he could change, but because his wife had said, with tears in her eyes, that she missed him. And he realized, with a hollow ache, that he missed himself too. He hoped, more than he dared to admit, that there might be a way to feel safe without having to stay so hidden.
